register.name: International bond due 2037
register.detail: Priced 10 September 2026 · Closed 17 September 2026 · Coupon 6.25% · Repaid in three instalments
register.note: Orders of about two and a half times the amount on offer
register.text: A US$1 billion bond sold in the international capital markets less than a year after Hurricane Melissa. Part of the proceeds bought back older notes due 2028, 2036 and 2039. Cheaper, longer debt leaves more of the budget for the seven standards.

register.name: UN Central Emergency Response Fund, Hurricane Melissa
register.detail: Additional allocation confirmed 26 November 2025 · UNICEF, IOM, PAHO/WHO and WFP
register.note: Water for more than 220,000 people; health care for 600,000
register.text: An additional US$4 million from the UN Central Emergency Response Fund for the hardest-hit parishes. It pays for emergency shelter for 8,800 people, cash for food for 10,756, safe water and sanitation for more than 220,000, and essential health care for 600,000. It reaches food, water, shelter and health at once.

register.name: CAF emergency grant, Hurricane Melissa
register.text: An emergency grant from CAF, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, approved five days after the storm. It supports the Government’s relief work alongside other partners.

register.name: IFRC emergency appeal, Hurricane Melissa
register.detail: Launched 30 October 2025 · 24 months · CHF 19 million (about $23 million)
register.note: 180,000 people, relief and recovery over two years
register.text: The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies appeal for 180,000 people in ten of the most affected parishes. It pays for shelter repair and reconstruction, safe drinking water, hygiene, medical care and the recovery of livelihoods.

register.name: Catastrophe bond, 2026
register.detail: Priced 18 May 2026 · Settled 26 May 2026 · Matures 23 May 2030 · Risk margin 6.75% a year
register.note: Pays out when a severe hurricane meets the trigger
register.text: A World Bank catastrophe bond that gives Jamaica $200 million of parametric cover against named storms until May 2030, replacing the $150 million of cover Hurricane Melissa triggered. Investors in Europe, North America and Bermuda oversubscribed it, so the target was raised. Money that arrives within weeks of a storm protects food, shelter and livelihoods while the country rebuilds.

register.name: ADAPT Jamaica (FP299)
register.detail: Approved at the 44th meeting of the GCF Board · Funded Activity Agreement signed 28 March 2026 · Grant through FAO
register.note: More than 700,000 people in six central parishes
register.text: A Green Climate Fund project, with the Food and Agriculture Organization, that helps smallholders in central Jamaica withstand climate shocks. It pays for farmer field schools, solar-powered irrigation, cold storage, water harvesting and hurricane-resilient protected agriculture. It serves the food and livelihood standards.

register.name: Rapid Financing Instrument, large natural disaster window
register.detail: Approved 16 January 2026 · SDR 306.32 million · 80 percent of quota
register.note: Urgent balance-of-payments needs after Hurricane Melissa
register.text: An IMF disbursement of about US$415 million to meet the urgent balance-of-payments needs caused by Hurricane Melissa. It complements Jamaica’s layered disaster risk financing, which the IMF found insufficient on its own for a storm of this size.

register.name: Catastrophe bond, 2024
register.detail: Renewed May 2024 · Triggered by Hurricane Melissa, October 2025 · Paid out in full
register.text: The $150 million World Bank catastrophe bond renewed in May 2024 was fully triggered by Hurricane Melissa, which struck on 28 October 2025. Investors paid Jamaica the whole principal within weeks of the storm.

register.name: CCRIF parametric insurance payouts, Hurricane Melissa
register.detail: Tropical cyclone $70.8 million, 31 October 2025 · Excess rainfall $21.1 million, 6 November 2025
register.note: The largest single payout CCRIF has made
register.text: Two payouts from the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility, both made within 14 days of the storm: J$14.8 billion in all. The tropical cyclone payout is the largest in CCRIF’s history.

register.name: Sustainable and Resilient Recovery Development Policy Financing
register.detail: Approved 3 March 2025 · IBRD · $150 million budget support and a $42 million Cat DDO
register.note: Budget support and a contingent credit line for disasters
register.text: World Bank budget support for reforms in trade, digital services and the financial sector, with a Catastrophe Deferred Drawdown Option that Jamaica can draw quickly after a disaster. The reforms set up a National Natural Disaster Reserve Fund, raise building codes for hospitals and shelters, and encourage household solar panels.

register.name: Contingent Loan for Natural Disaster Emergencies, Hurricane Melissa (JA-L1099)
register.detail: Approved 1 July 2026 · Sovereign-guaranteed investment loan · In implementation
register.note: Fast contingent finance for emergency public spending
register.text: An Inter-American Development Bank loan that finances the Government’s response to Hurricane Melissa from contingent resources, so that emergency spending does not strain the budget. In November 2025 the IDB had expanded Jamaica’s contingent credit line to up to US$300 million.

register.name: Southern Plains Agricultural Development Project, additional financing
register.detail: Announced 9 April 2026 · Concessional loan, Special Development Fund · Completion by 2028
register.note: Irrigation and packhouses at Amity Hall and Parnassus
register.text: Caribbean Development Bank financing to finish a UK Caribbean Infrastructure Fund project that replaces flood irrigation with climate-resilient water systems in the southern plains. It pays for irrigation at Amity Hall, packhouses in St Catherine and Clarendon, and support for farmers. It serves the food and livelihood standards.

register.name: Continued Public Sector Transformation Programme
register.detail: Approved November 2025 · Signed 13 February 2026 · 23.5 years, 7 years’ grace · Programme $78.5 million
register.note: Shared services, payroll and procurement across government
register.text: An IDB loan, with $8.5 million from the Government, that brings shared corporate services, digital human resources and payroll, and simpler procurement to the public service over about six years. Savings are to be moved to priority areas.

register.name: Rio Cobre Water Treatment Plant
register.detail: Signed 13 December 2024 · Up to 20 years · 15 million imperial gallons a day · Completion due May 2027
register.note: Water for more than 600,000 people in Kingston and St Catherine
register.text: A public-private partnership between the National Water Commission and Rio Cobre Water Limited, financed by a $30 million IDB Invest loan and $49 million from Proparco, Sagicor Bank Jamaica and the Development Bank of Jamaica. The plant will treat 15 million imperial gallons a day for Kingston, Portmore and Spanish Town. It serves the water standard.

items.name: The People
items.label: Citizens, 2025
items.text: 59 in every hundred live in towns and cities; the rest live on the land they farm and fish.
items.alt: A busy street in Kingston, Jamaica

items.name: The Land
items.label: Of land in farms and pasture
items.text: The land that feeds the nation, and the first place a citizen dividend can be earned.
items.alt: Farmland in the hills of the Jamaican interior

items.name: The Forest
items.label: Of land under forest
items.text: Standing forest holds the water, soil and carbon that the world will pay to keep.
items.alt: Forest on the slopes of the Blue Mountains, Jamaica

items.name: The Water
items.label: Renewable fresh water per person
items.text: Enough to supply every home, once it is stored, treated and piped.
items.alt: A waterfall on a river in Jamaica

items.name: The Power
items.label: Of energy from renewables, 2021
items.text: Sun, wind, water and biomass already carry part of the load; the rest is the opportunity.
items.alt: Wind turbines on a ridge in Jamaica

items.name: Jamaica Public Service Company (JPS)
items.text: The island’s electricity utility, which spent more than US$300 million restoring generation, transmission and distribution after Hurricane Melissa. IDB Invest is considering up to US$80 million for its recovery and grid hardening.

items.name: JMMB Bank
items.text: A Jamaican bank lending to small and medium enterprises and to low- and middle-income home buyers. IDB Invest lent it up to US$35 million, with technical help for women-led businesses.
